Abstract
With the increasing demand for secure multimedia data transmission, chaotic systems have attracted widespread attention 
due to their sensitivity to initial conditions and pseudo-randomness. However, traditional low-dimensional chaotic systems 
often suffer from limited complexity and predictability, making them insufficient for high-security image encryption appli-
cations. To enhance the practicality and security of chaotic systems in the field of image encryption, this paper proposes a 
novel four-dimensional multi-scroll multi-wing hyperchaotic system and a corresponding color image encryption algorithm 
incorporating a DNA mutation mechanism. First, A nonlinear coupling term and an external periodic modulation factor are 
introduced into the Lorenz system to construct a four-dimensional multi-scroll multi-wing hyperchaotic system. This system 
features 16-wing symmetric attractors, time-varying equilibrium points, and complex dynamical behavior. Its hyperchaotic 
properties and nonlinear evolution characteristics are validated using Lyapunov exponent spectra, bifurcation diagrams, phase 
portraits, and Poincaré sections. Subsequently, based on this system, a DNA-based image encryption framework is proposed 
by combining DNA computing with gene mutation mechanisms. The encryption scheme includes two-level scrambling, 
self-feedback, inter-channel cross diffusion, and a key-controlled DNA mutation module. Experimental results show that 
the algorithm achieves excellent performance in information entropy, NPCR/UACI, and key sensitivity, demonstrating its 
effectiveness and robustness for image information protection.

1  Introduction

2024, 2022a, 2022b). Due to the large volume, high redun-

difficult to meet the demands of high-strength information 
protection. Chaotic systems, characterized by their sensitiv-
ity to initial conditions, unpredictability of trajectories, and 
flexible parameter control (Xian et al. 2024), possess excel-
lent pseudo-randomness and complex dynamic behavior, 
offering inherent advantages in image encryption. Chaos-
based encryption methods can effectively disrupt the spatial 
distribution of image pixels and construct large key spaces 
by adjusting initial values and system parameters, thereby

In recent years, as the application value of multi-wing 
chaotic systems has become increasingly prominent in 
image encryption and secure communications, researchers 
have continuously extended classical systems to develop 
novel multi-wing chaotic systems with more complex 
structures and diverse attractor geometries. Ye and He 
(Ye and He 2024) introduced a nonlinear control function 
and an improved feedback term to construct a novel three-
dimensional continuous-time multi-scroll chaotic system, 
and successfully verified its advantages in tunable attractor 
structures and practical implementation via circuit simu-
lation. Sahoo and Roy (Sahoo and Roy 2022) proposed a 
multi-wing chaotic system whose number of attractors can 
be dynamically adjusted by system parameters, showcas-
ing the diversity of attractor structures under multiple ini-
tial conditions and parameter settings. Yan et al. (Yan et al. 
2024) further developed a method for controlling the geo-
metric structure of attractors, enabling smooth transitions 
from “dart-shaped” to “circular” forms, thereby enhancing 
the geometric plasticity of chaotic systems. Yu et al. (Yu 
et al. 2024) constructed a five-dimensional fractional-order 
chaotic system with memristors and multi-parameter cou-
pling, exhibiting both multi-wing and hidden attractor fea-
tures, and implemented it on FPGA hardware. Yang et al. 
(Yang et al. 2022) developed a three-dimensional sine-based 
system capable of generating multistable and multi-scroll 
attractor structures, suitable for secure communication and 
random number generation. Wu et al. (Wu et al. 2020) pro-
posed an amplitude control mechanism to flexibly construct 
butterfly-shaped and nested attractors, improving the tun-
ability of attractor morphologies. Yan et al. (Yan et al. 2021) 
designed a double-wing chaotic system with infinite equilib-
rium points and coexisting rotational attractors, which can 
be used in precise applications such as weak signal detec-
tion. Azzaz et al. (Azzaz et al. 2021) developed a multi-wing 
attractor based on the Lorenz system for high-quality true 
random number generation and achieved hardware imple-
mentation via FPGA. Sambas et al. (Sambas et al. 2020) 
built a three-dimensional multistable chaotic system based 
on a peanut-shaped equilibrium curve, which demonstrates 
high symmetry and complexity.
With the deep integration of chaos theory and DNA com-
puting in the field of information security, image encryption 
algorithms combining chaotic systems and DNA operations 
have become a research hotspot. Yan et al. (Yan et al. 2025) 
developed a three-dimensional conservative chaotic system 
for color image encryption, where dynamic DNA encod-
ing was used to implement pixel perturbation and diffusion, 
significantly enhancing key sensitivity and image security. 
Alawida et al. (Alawida 2024) combined DNA tree struc-
tures with three-dimensional chaotic maps, employing 
multi-branch DNA computations for pixel scrambling and 
introducing a differential chaos mechanism to control key 
generation and diffusion. Chen et al. (Chen et al. 2024) pro-
posed an image encryption scheme based on an improved 
two-dimensional logistic mapping and algebraic DNA com-
puting, which enhances pixel scrambling and diffusion pro-
cesses, thereby improving resistance to conventional attacks 
and strengthening overall encryption security. Hao et al. 
(Hao et al. 2021) proposed an image encryption scheme 
based on a five-dimensional fractional-order chaotic sys-
tem, utilizing DNA mutation mechanisms for multi-round 
encoding and diffusion to strengthen dynamic complexity 
and attack resistance. Liu and Ye (Liu and Ye 2021) devel-
oped an image encryption model that integrates a hyper-
chaotic system with an asymmetric key mechanism, adopt-
ing nonlinear DNA operations to achieve high-intensity 
pixel-level disturbance and diffusion. Roy et al. (Roy et al. 
2021) designed an encryption framework that combines 
DNA encoding with chaotic perturbation, enhancing sys-
tem robustness through dynamic mapping and XOR-based 
diffusion. Wan et al. (Wan et al. 2020) further combined 
compound chaos and hyperchaotic systems to generate high-
dimensional nonlinear key streams and employed multi-
round DNA scrambling and diffusion mechanisms to effec-
tively enhance the security performance of the algorithm.
Although multi-wing chaotic systems have been widely 
applied in image encryption in recent years, and their 
complex attractor structures help enhance the randomness 
and unpredictability of key sequences, most existing sys-
tems suffer from low dimensionality and limited nonlinear 
dynamic behaviors. These limitations hinder the generation 
of larger key spaces and more intricate dynamic patterns, 
thereby restricting the overall security strength of encryp-
tion schemes. On the other hand, current DNA-based image 
encryption algorithms typically rely on fixed encoding rules 
and static logical operations, lacking the ability to model 
real biological DNA mutation behaviors. As a result, the 
disturbance process remains relatively simple and fails to 
replicate the high complexity and irreversibility observed 
in natural biological systems, which reduces the robustness 
of the encryption scheme against differential attacks and 
statistical analysis.
To address these limitations, this paper proposes a novel 
color image encryption algorithm that combines a four-
dimensional multi-scroll multi-wing hyperchaotic sys-
tem—to expand the key space and improve chaotic behav-
ior—with a DNA mutation mechanism that more accurately 
simulates natural biological processes, thereby enhancing 
both the complexity and security robustness of the encryp-
tion procedure.

hyperchaotic system is constructed, capable of gener-
ating complex attractors with 16 wings. The system

2  DNA mechanisms for image encryption
This section introduces the core DNA mechanisms adopted 
in the proposed image encryption scheme, including binary-
to-DNA encoding rules, base-level arithmetic operations, 
and key-controlled gene mutation strategies. These mecha-
nisms not only provide symbolic representations of binary 
data but also serve as fundamental tools for pixel distur-
bance and diffusion, enhancing the nonlinearity, diffusion 
effect, and statistical balance of the encryption process. 
The resulting ciphertext gains improved randomness and 
unpredictability.
2.1  DNA encoding
Deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) is the molecular carrier of 
genetic information in living organisms. It consists of four 
types of nitrogenous bases: adenine (A), cytosine (C), gua-
nine (G), and thymine (T). Among them, A pairs with T and 
C pairs with G through stable complementary base pairing 
(Watson and Crick 1953). In the context of information rep-
resentation, binary encoding consists solely of 0 and 1. Since 
any two-bit binary combination yields four unique patterns, 
this coincides with the number of DNA bases. Considering 
base complementarity, every 2-bit binary number can be 
mapped to a DNA base to form a DNA encoding scheme.

2.3  Gene mutation
In molecular genetics, gene mutation refers to the alteration 
of the composition or arrangement of bases within a DNA 
sequence. These mutations typically manifest in the form of 
base substitution, insertion, deletion, or sequence inversion 
(Griffiths et al. 2020). Such changes may not only result in 
abnormal gene expression or alterations in protein structure 
(Li et al. 2019), but also significantly affect the way informa-
tion is interpreted and transmitted, reflecting the high plasticity 
and complexity of DNA sequences in terms of information 
representation. From an information theory perspective, even 
minor mutations in base sequences can lead to substantial 
changes in the encoded output. This sensitivity and nonlin-
ear mapping behavior provide a theoretical foundation for the 
design of interference resistance and confusion mechanisms 
in encryption systems. Based on this insight, this paper pro-
poses a DNA mutation-based image encryption algorithm 
that simulates naturally occurring point mutations, frameshift 
mutations, and inversion mutations in DNA molecules through 
a combination of base substitution, positional perturbation, and 
sequence inversion operations.
3  Four‑dimensional multi‑scroll multi‑wing 
hyperchaotic system
This Section investigates a newly developed four-dimen-
sional multi-scroll multi-wing hyperchaotic system. Based 
on the classical Lorenz system, the proposed model incor-
porates nonlinear coupling terms and an external periodic 
modulation mechanism, resulting in significantly enriched 
dynamical behaviors. Notably, the system exhibits a 
16-wing symmetric attractor with intricate multi-wing 
distributions and features time-dependent, non-fixed 
equilibrium points, highlighting its unique evolution-
ary dynamics under a non-autonomous framework and 
periodic driving. A comprehensive dynamical analysis 
is conducted using Lyapunov exponents, phase portraits, 
bifurcation diagrams, Poincaré sections, and sensitivity 
to initial conditions. The results confirm the system’s 
hyperchaotic nature, high sensitivity to initial perturba-
tions, and typical nonlinear evolutionary characteristics, 
thereby establishing a solid theoretical foundation for its 
application in image encryption and broader information 
security domains.

In the study of dynamical systems, dissipativity is a key 
property used to assess the long-term behavior of chaotic 
systems. A system is considered dissipative if the volume 
of its phase space contracts over time, meaning that system 
trajectories do not diverge indefinitely but are instead con-
fined within a bounded region—typically an attractor. For 
the chaotic system proposed in this paper, its dissipativity is 
evaluated using Eq. (4).
When the system parameters are set as described above, 
the divergence ∇V = −15, indicating that the system is dis-

Vx will decay exponentially as Vx = e−15t, and rapidly shrink 
to zero. As t →∞ , the phase space volume elements of the

eventually be confined within a low-dimensional attractor.

3.2.4  Lyapunov exponents and Kaplan–Yorke dimension

the stability and chaotic behavior of dynamical systems. 
They quantitatively describe the divergence rate between 
nearby trajectories and reflect the system’s sensitivity to ini-
tial conditions. If at least one Lyapunov exponent is positive, 
the system is considered to exhibit chaotic behavior; con-
versely, if all exponents are negative, the system trajectories 
tend to converge to a stable state.

5.3  Complexity and time efficiency analysis
Although the proposed image encryption algorithm incurs 
relatively high computational costs during the encryption 
and decryption phases, such overhead is the necessary 
price for implementing a multi-layered security mecha-
nism. To better reveal the algorithm’s performance charac-
teristics under the security design, this section analyzes it 
from the perspectives of theoretical complexity and actual 
time efficiency.
5.3.1  Complexity analysis
The proposed image encryption algorithm comprises mul-
tiple serial processing modules, with overall complexity 
depending on the number of operations in each module rela-
tive to the image size. Let the plaintext image size be M × N, 
and the total number of pixels be n = M × N.
In the key stream generation stage, the four-dimensional 
hyperchaotic system is iterated L + 3n times to obtain cha-
otic sequences. Since each iteration is a constant-time opera-
tion, the time complexity for this stage is O(n). During the 
dual-stage pixel scrambling, the sorting-based permutation 
requires flattening the 2D pixel matrix of each channel and 
sorting it, yielding a complexity of O(nlogn). The Arnold 
mapping, being a fixed-number linear mapping, has a com-
plexity of O(n). In the diffusion stage, the key is used to 
perform self-feedback XOR operations on the three-channel 
pixel vector sequentially, which is a linear operation with 
O(n) complexity. The DNA encoding stage assigns each 
pixel one encoding operation followed by one DNA com-
putation, resulting in O(n) complexity. The genetic mutation 
perturbation phase includes base substitution, shifting, and 
inversion operations, all executable in constant time, thus 
also O(n). Finally, DNA decoding, as the inverse process of 
encoding, maintains linear complexity.
In summary, except for the sorting operation, all modules 
have linear complexity. Therefore, the overall time complex-
ity of the proposed algorithm is O(nlogn).
5.3.2  Execution time
Building on the theoretical complexity analysis, we further 
evaluate the practical time efficiency of the proposed image 
encryption scheme through experiments. All experiments 
were conducted on a laptop equipped with an Apple M1 Pro 
processor, 16 GB RAM, and macOS Monterey 12.5, using 
MATLAB R2021b as the simulation platform.
As shown in Table 19, for images sized 256 × 256, the 
encryption time is approximately 65–66 s, and decryption 
takes about 51–52 s. For images sized 512 × 512, encryption 
time increases to 260–283 s, while decryption takes 209–224 
s, demonstrating a growth trend consistent with the theoreti-
cal complexity.
The main computational cost arises from the multi-stage 
processing pipeline, including key generation, sorting-based 
scrambling, dynamic DNA encoding, and genetic pertur-
bation—all designed for high-security purposes. Although 
the runtime is relatively long, this is a deliberate trade-off 
to ensure strong resistance to attacks and high encryption 
strength for sensitive image data. In this study, security is 
prioritized over processing speed, making this computa-
tional burden acceptable in applications with high security 
requirements.
Future work will focus on improving efficiency while pre-
serving security. On one hand, image partitioning and par-
allel processing strategies using multi-core CPUs or GPUs 
could significantly reduce overall runtime by performing 
scrambling, diffusion, and DNA operations concurrently. 
On the other hand, optimizing key generation logic, DNA 
computation lookups, and employing vectorized operations 
may further reduce time and resource consumption.

Abstract: With the increasing demand for secure multimedia data transmission, chaotic systems have attracted widespread attention due to their sensitivity to initial conditions and pseudo-randomness. However, traditional low-dimensional chaotic systems often suffer from limited complexity and predictability, making them insufficient for high-security image encryption appli- cations. To enhance the practicality and security of chaotic systems in the field of image encryption, this paper proposes a novel four-dimensional multi-scroll multi-wing hyperchaotic system and a corresponding color image encryption algorithm incorporating a DNA mutation mechanism. First, A nonlinear coupling term and an external periodic modulation factor are introduced into the Lorenz system to construct a four-dimensional multi-scroll multi-wing hyperchaotic system. This system features 16-wing symmetric attractors, time-varying equilibrium points, and complex dynamical behavior. Its hyperchaotic properties and nonlinear evolution characteristics are validated using Lyapunov exponent spectra, bifurcation diagrams, phase portraits, and Poincaré sections. Subsequently, based on this system, a DNA-based image encryption framework is proposed by combining DNA computing with gene mutation mechanisms. The encryption scheme includes two-level scrambling, self-feedback, inter-channel cross diffusion, and a key-controlled DNA mutation module. Experimental results show that the algorithm achieves excellent performance in information entropy, NPCR/UACI, and key sensitivity, demonstrating its effectiveness and robustness for image information protection.
